newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian business calls on Abacha to privatise.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian business calls on Abacha to privatise.

text.p: Nigeria's manufacturers on Monday sent an appeal to military ruler General Sani Abacha bemoaning the decay of national utilities and calling for faster privatisation as a long term solution.

The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, which groups all the biggest private manufacturing businesses, said the progressive collapse of state-run services had forced up costs and was making it ever more difficult to make money.

"Unless action is taken now, the key objective of the 1997 budget to achieve sustainable growth and development with a target annual growth of 5.5 percent will not be realised," the message to Abacha said.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation of over 100 million people, has languished in recession since political and economic turmoil erupted in the wake of annulled 1993 elections.

Relative financial stability has been restored by Abacha, who took power in the chaos, but the business climate has grown ever harsher with the failure of petrol supplies, electricity and communications -- all dependent on state-run utilities.
"General commerce has been impaired and the problem of low sales by industries has been accentuated as evidenced by warehouses that are brimming with a backlog of unsold goods," the message said.

Businesses can set up their own generating plants when power stations fail, but the inability of oil refineries to satisfy local demand leaves firms with no choice but to wait for the erratic supplies or close up shop.
Local newspapers dubbed weeks of fuel shortage which paralysed Nigeria earlier in the year a "national shame" in Africa's biggest crude oil producer.

"In the final anaylsis government should give serious thought to accelerating the pace of its privatisation programme," the message said. "This is of particular relevance to electricity and the refineries."

Nigeria's ruling generals have so far resisted pressure from business and foreign lenders to privatise. Nothing has been heard publicly from a promised commission, which was to investigate the practicalities of privatisation.

The apparent reluctance to privatise has become another sticking point in relations with Western countries that were already unhappy about alleged human rights abuses and suspicious of Abacha's plan to restore civilian rule in 1998.

Business and political analysts say the issue is too closely entwined with the military and regional interests on which Nigerian politics revolves to be able to find a simple way out -- even if services suffer.

"Since infrastructure is the foundation for sustainable growth and development, everything should be done to guarantee adequate and efficient delivery of utility services," the message from the manufacturers said.
